By March, Swati noticed that her life in the Kolkata flat had become a loop: office, metro, dinner, phone, sleep. She wasn't sad, just dull, and she didn't want to drift for another year.
So she made three small changes. She got off the metro one stop early and walked along the lake. She signed up for Saturday tabla lessons with an old teacher in the next lane. And once a month she cooked a big meal for her flatmate Jaya and two neighbours. The tabla was humbling; her fingers ached. But Saturdays had a shape again.
She also made herself a quiet promise, written in her phone notes: if the dullness turned heavy and stayed, she would see a doctor, not just wait.

At the residential school outside the small town of Sagar, lights went out at ten. Zainab lay on the top bunk listening to the ceiling fan click. At home right now, Ammi would be rolling rotis for tomorrow, Abbu's radio would be playing old songs, and her little brother would be arguing about homework. Here there was only the fan and Reena breathing below.
Zainab pressed her face into the pillow so she wouldn't sniff. In the morning Reena asked, "You slept okay?" "Like a rock," Zainab said brightly. She didn't want to be the Class 9 girl who cried for her Ammi. At breakfast the dal had no hing, and she missed home so much her throat hurt.
